reference.source: Williams Hematology / Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
clinicalPearls: A group of inherited anaemias characterised by ineffective erythropoiesis and morphologically abnormal, often multinucleated, erythroblasts in the marrow
Type I (CDAN1 or C15orf41) shows megaloblastoid erythroblasts with internuclear chromatin bridges; type II (SEC23B), the commonest, shows binucleate late erythroblasts
Type II is also known as HEMPAS, in which red cells lyse in a proportion of acidified normal sera and show characteristic membrane glycoprotein abnormalities
The anaemia is typically macrocytic or normocytic with inappropriately low reticulocytes for the degree of anaemia
Iron overload is common and progresses even without transfusion because ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin
Splenomegaly and jaundice from haemolysis of the abnormal cells are frequent, and gallstones may develop
Diagnosis rests on marrow morphology plus genetic testing, distinguishing CDA from thalassaemia and myelodysplasia
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemias are disorders of terminal erythroid maturation in which erythroblasts undergo abnormal nuclear division and cytokinesis, generating characteristic multinucleate and internuclear-bridged forms. The underlying genes govern nuclear envelope integrity and chromatin organisation (CDAN1 in type I), endoplasmic reticulum vesicle transport and glycoprotein processing (SEC23B in type II), and erythroid transcription or cytokinesis machinery in rarer subtypes. Defective maturation leads to apoptosis of erythroid precursors within the marrow, producing ineffective erythropoiesis with a low reticulocyte response relative to the anaemia. As with other ineffective erythropoieses, expanded but futile erythroid activity suppresses hepcidin and drives excess intestinal iron absorption, so tissue iron overload accumulates independently of transfusion.
additionalDifferentials: Megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
Congenital haemolytic anaemias such as hereditary spherocytosis
additionalInvestigations: Bone marrow aspirate examining erythroblast multinuclearity and chromatin bridges
Full blood count, reticulocyte count, and blood film to characterise the anaemia
Haemolysis markers including bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, and haptoglobin
Iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation) and hepatic iron quantification by MRI
Targeted genetic testing (CDAN1, C15orf41, SEC23B, KLF1, KIF23)
Electron microscopy of erythroblasts in selected cases to define subtype
redFlags: Signs of iron overload affecting heart, liver, or endocrine organs even without transfusion
Severe anaemia in infancy requiring frequent transfusion
Hydrops or profound anaemia detected antenatally in severe variants
Progressive cytopenias or dysplasia raising concern for an alternative marrow disorder
reference.prognosis: Many patients have a moderate, compatible-with-life anaemia, but long-term morbidity is dominated by iron overload and its organ complications, making iron monitoring and chelation central to care regardless of transfusion status.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the marrow appearances as myelodysplasia and pursuing inappropriate therapy
Failing to monitor and treat iron overload in non-transfused patients
Confusing the macrocytosis with B12 or folate deficiency and missing the congenital cause
Overlooking the diagnosis in a family member with milder compensated disease
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
